title: When AI Becomes a Colleague: The Future of India's Legal Profession
pub: Observer Research Foundation (Expert Speak / Young Voices)
author: Sairah Zahoor

dom.t: Public justice: AI access requires accountable adjudication

st.t: Machine judging: Accuracy cannot establish legitimate authority
st.an: The source does not address whether technical accuracy can legitimate autonomous judicial authority. It redirects attention to a different institutional issue: how uneven AI adoption and the loss of repetitive junior work may reshape the development of lawyers’ professional judgement.
qs: The consequence is not that lawyers become redundant, but that the profession’s primary mechanism for producing professional judgement is beginning to change.

For India's over one million enrolled advocates, most outside the small tier of AI-equipped commercial firms, the question is no longer whether generative AI will be used but how unevenly its costs and benefits will be distributed.

st.t: AI instruction: Timing divides educational reform
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core proposition that legal education must develop independent judgment alongside practical AI competence. It materially extends the synthesis through an Indian legal-education perspective, defining AI supervision as a discrete professional competency and arguing that schools must deliberately replace apprenticeship opportunities lost when AI absorbs junior work.
qs: ## Competency Redefined  If junior lawyers no longer learn by doing the volume of work AI now performs, legal education must deliberately supply what apprenticeship once supplied by accident.
> AI supervision is becoming a discrete professional competency, not a passive byproduct of new software.

st.t: Court responsibility: AI requires lifecycle supervision
st.an: The source accepts the need for human verification, advisory-only AI and retained judicial responsibility, then materially extends the cluster with India-specific evidence that judicial safeguards are advancing faster than professional regulation. It identifies gaps in bar guidance and confidentiality protection while cautioning that court technology pilots do not yet demonstrate backlog reduction.
qs: The Bar Council’s own Standards of Professional Conduct, framed before large language models existed, remain silent on AI delegation and verification duties.

st.t: Firm adoption: Access outruns dependable integration
st.an: The source accepts that firm-level AI adoption has consequences beyond tool access and extends the cluster with India-specific mechanisms: fixed-fee incentives may undermine junior training, while adoption concentrated in large commercial firms may widen unequal access. These are mainly argued or predicted effects rather than measured firm-wide productivity or justice outcomes.
qs: As clients resist paying by the hour for work AI can automate, fixed-fee arrangements are gaining ground, narrowing the revenue that once funded junior lawyers' training.
Smaller practitioners and legal aid organisations such as [NALSA](https://nalsa.gov.in/) remain outside the AI ecosystem, widening an already significant access-to-justice gap.

st.t: Judgment development: AI exposure is not professional readiness
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core distinction between AI exposure and professional readiness, arguing that teaching AI as a subject is insufficient without deliberate training in independent judgment, verification and supervision. It materially extends the synthesis through an India-specific proposal to make competence in interrogating and overruling AI-generated work a condition of enrolment, while linking that training need to automation’s erosion of traditional apprenticeship opportunities.
qs: The Bar Council of India has [directed](https://www.pib.gov.in/PressReleaseIframePage.aspx?PRID=2040667&reg=48&lang=2) universities to incorporate artificial intelligence into their curricula, but adding AI as a subject differs from training lawyers to supervise, interrogate and overrule it.
The Bar Council's curriculum mandate should move beyond teaching AI as a subject and require competence in verifying, interrogating and overruling AI-generated work before enrolment.

st.t: Justice access: Direct AI use shifts risk downward
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s concern that AI benefits may concentrate among well-resourced providers and materially extends it with India-specific proposals: shared public infrastructure for legal-aid and solo practices, verification competence for lawyers, and court deployment assessed by backlog reduction. It focuses more on provider inequality and supervised institutional use than on direct-to-consumer risk.
qs: A government-backed shared AI infrastructure scheme, channelled through NALSA and state legal services authorities, would extend tools concentrated in large firms to legal aid providers and solo practitioners, keeping the access-to-justice gap from widening further.
The Bar Council's curriculum mandate should move beyond teaching AI as a subject and require competence in verifying, interrogating and overruling AI-generated work before enrolment.

st.t: Law-firm pyramid: Efficiency threatens revenue and training
st.an: Zahoor accepts the cluster’s core account: AI compresses junior production, weakens the hourly-billing mechanism that financed apprenticeship, and is more likely to narrow junior hiring and shift skills than eliminate lawyers. She materially extends it with an India-specific distributional and policy analysis, proposing verification-focused education and shared public AI infrastructure to prevent smaller practices and legal-aid providers from falling further behind.
qs: As clients resist paying by the hour for work AI can automate, fixed-fee arrangements are gaining ground, narrowing the revenue that once funded junior lawyers' training.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core account that AI is reconfiguring legal work rather than replacing lawyers, while creating verification and apprenticeship risks. It materially extends the synthesis with an India-specific institutional agenda covering professional discipline, legal education, shared infrastructure, confidentiality and judicial deployment.
qs: The consequence is not that lawyers become redundant, but that the profession’s primary mechanism for producing professional judgement is beginning to change.

The question is not whether lawyers will use AI, but whether India's legal institutions will act on the gaps identified here — in verification, education and access — before the profession is reshaped by default rather than by design.

st.t: Legal workforce: Junior pipelines face the sharpest risk
st.an: Zahoor accepts the cluster’s core view that AI will restructure legal work rather than eliminate lawyers, while identifying junior apprenticeship and hiring as the principal risk. She materially extends the synthesis with India-specific adoption evidence and a distributional warning that unequal access may widen the justice gap.

st.an: Zahoor accepts the cluster’s public-justice and accountable-adjudication framing, while materially extending it with concrete proposals for professional competence in supervising AI, enforceable verification duties, confidentiality reform and shared public infrastructure for legal-aid providers and solo practitioners.

st.t: Supervised AI: Verification may consume efficiency gains
st.an: Zahoor accepts the cluster’s supervised-AI proposition and materially develops it for India. She frames AI as augmenting rather than replacing legal judgment, then proposes concrete institutional responses: enforceable citation verification, authenticated domestic databases, AI-supervision training, disclosure duties and stronger confidentiality protections. Her apprenticeship and access-to-justice concerns also reinforce the cluster’s warnings about preserving human capability and unevenly distributed benefits.
qs: In law, this suggests AI's value lies in supporting judgement, not replacing it, provided lawyers evaluate its output critically rather than accept it wholesale.

The Bar Council should adopt the disciplinary rules the Supreme Court has directed it to frame, making independent verification of every AI-sourced citation a precondition of filing, backed by investment in authenticated domestic legal databases so verification does not depend on proprietary systems beyond domestic reach.

st.t: Task substitution: Complementarity can still reshape staffing
st.an: Zahoor accepts that AI substitutes for recurring legal tasks while complementing human judgement, and predicts that this will reshape rather than eliminate legal employment. She materially extends the proposition by connecting reduced junior drafting roles to apprenticeship funding, AI-supervision roles, verification-focused education and unequal access within India’s legal profession.
qs: The consequence is not that lawyers become redundant, but that the profession’s primary mechanism for producing professional judgement is beginning to change.
Large firms will keep hiring junior associates, but fewer of them and for narrower purposes, as AI-supervision and legal-technology roles expand.

st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core claim that AI is restructuring legal-service production rather than eliminating lawyers. kp.k: Automation threatens apprenticeship rather than making all lawyers redundant
kp.d: Zahoor argues that drafting contracts and summarising case files traditionally developed professional judgement through supervised repetition. Generative AI increasingly performs that formative work, changing how lawyers acquire judgement rather than necessarily eliminating lawyers. The conclusion warns that no institution has yet replaced what apprenticeship taught.
qs: The consequence is not that lawyers become redundant, but that the profession’s primary mechanism for producing professional judgement is beginning to change.
What is changing is not simply how lawyers work but how they become lawyers at all.

kp.k: Pricing changes threaten the subsidy for junior training
kp.d: The author links client resistance to hourly charges for automatable work and growing fixed-fee use to reduced funding for associate apprenticeship. She reports that the Thomson Reuters 2025 Future of Professionals report found 80 percent of respondents expected AI to change pricing, staffing and delivery, while roughly 90 percent of corporate outside-counsel spending remained hourly. These figures concern expectations and billing prevalence, not measured training losses.
qs: Legal training has long been subsidised by billing.
As clients resist paying by the hour for work AI can automate, fixed-fee arrangements are gaining ground, narrowing the revenue that once funded junior lawyers' training.
When billing stops rewarding volume, firms stop generating volume for juniors to learn from.

kp.k: Enterprise adoption concentrates benefits among large Indian firms
kp.d: The article reports AZB & Partners' firm-wide Harvey AI rollout in September 2025 for document review and translation, following Shardul Amarchand Mangaldas' earlier partnership. It also reports Harvey's Bengaluru office and a legal-services market projection of US$67.4 billion by 2030. Against India's over one million enrolled advocates, the author argues that smaller practitioners and legal aid organisations such as NALSA remain outside this ecosystem, potentially widening unmet legal need.
qs: These gains concentrate among large commercial firms.
Smaller practitioners and legal aid organisations such as NALSA remain outside the AI ecosystem, widening an already significant access-to-justice gap.

kp.k: Junior hiring shifts toward supervision and technology roles
kp.d: Reporting the International Bar Association's observation that automation first affects tasks previously assigned to juniors, Zahoor predicts fewer drafting associates and earlier responsibility for supervising AI output. Over the next decade, she expects continued but reduced junior hiring, expanding AI-supervision and legal-technology roles, and sustained premiums for specialist litigation, regulatory advisory and courtroom advocacy. These are forecasts rather than documented employment outcomes.
qs: Hiring will likely shift toward fewer associates for drafting and more for supervising AI output from the outset of their careers.
Large firms will keep hiring junior associates, but fewer of them and for narrower purposes, as AI-supervision and legal-technology roles expand.
Specialist litigation, regulatory advisory and courtroom advocacy, the work least reducible to pattern-matching, will retain its premium.

kp.k: Education must teach critical supervision, not merely AI
kp.d: The author distinguishes the Bar Council of India's direction to incorporate AI into university curricula from practical competence in supervising, interrogating and overruling outputs. She reports Indian pedagogical concerns that outsourcing reasoning prevents judgement formation, and an OECD analysis suggesting AI more often reshapes tasks than replaces workers where it complements human skills. Her recommendation is to require verification and critical supervision competence before enrolment.
qs: If junior lawyers no longer learn by doing the volume of work AI now performs, legal education must deliberately supply what apprenticeship once supplied by accident.
In law, this suggests AI's value lies in supporting judgement, not replacing it, provided lawyers evaluate its output critically rather than accept it wholesale.
The Bar Council's curriculum mandate should move beyond teaching AI as a subject and require competence in verifying, interrogating and overruling AI-generated work before enrolment.

kp.k: Fabricated citations expose lawyers' independent verification duties
kp.d: The article reports the Bengaluru Income Tax Appellate Tribunal recalling its Buckeye Trust order in December 2024 over nonexistent judgments apparently sourced through ChatGPT; withdrawal of a Delhi High Court petition in September 2025 after fabricated citations were exposed; and more than a hundred imaginary citations in a Supreme Court commercial appeal by early 2026. It further reports that in July 2026 the Supreme Court set aside a tribunal ruling relying on six fabricated precedents, held that even an iota of hallucinated material voids a decision, and directed disciplinary rules for unverified filings. These reported incidents underpin the author's argument for human verification, not a measured model error rate.
qs: Because every precedent’s authority must be independently verifiable, that burden falls on the lawyer, not the tool.
AI supervision is becoming a discrete professional competency, not a passive byproduct of new software.

kp.k: Judicial AI rules retain human decision-making and verification
kp.d: The article reports reconstitution of the Supreme Court AI Committee in December 2025 and publication of draft court AI regulations in June 2026. It describes the draft as requiring disclosure in pleadings, prohibiting AI case decisions and bail-eligibility assessments, and making outputs advisory until human verification. Separately, it reports that Kerala High Court issued the first binding Indian high-court AI policy in July 2025, barring AI use in district-judiciary findings or judgments. The author cautions that disclosure does not establish reliability.
qs: India’s courts have moved faster than the profession’s own regulators.

lawyers and litigants to disclose AI use in pleadings, bars AI from deciding cases or assessing bail eligibility, and treats all AI output as advisory pending human verification, though disclosure alone does not test the output's reliability.

kp.k: Court technology deployment has uncertain effects on pendency
kp.d: The source reports over five crore pending cases, more than 85 percent in district and subordinate courts; Adalat AI transcription operating in more than 4,000 courts; and 53.57 crore rupees earmarked under eCourts Phase III for tools including LegRAA legal-research support and Digital Courts 2.1 paperless case management. It notes that government submissions describe the latter tools as controlled pilots. Zahoor questions whether modernisation will reduce the lower courts' backlog and recommends binding rollout timelines measured against pendency reduction.
qs: Whether efficiency gains at the apex will ever reach the district and subordinate courts carrying most of the pendency burden, rather than merely modernising paperwork, remains an open question.

The Department of Justice and the eCourts Phase III programme should set a binding timeline for extending pilot tools such as LegRAA and Digital Courts 2.1 to the district and subordinate courts, where 85 percent of pending cases sit, with success measured by pendency reduction, not administrative efficiency.

kp.k: Professional conduct rules lag judicial safeguards
kp.d: Zahoor asserts that the Bar Council's pre-LLM professional standards lack AI delegation and verification duties. She contrasts this with ABA Formal Opinion 512, issued in July 2024, which she describes as establishing competence, confidentiality and supervision obligations for generative AI use. She recommends adopting the disciplinary rules reportedly directed by the Supreme Court, requiring independent verification of every AI-sourced citation before filing, and investing in authenticated domestic legal databases.
qs: The Bar Council’s own Standards of Professional Conduct, framed before large language models existed, remain silent on AI delegation and verification duties.
India's advocates have no equivalent, even as the judiciary regulates AI use more explicitly than the bar does.

The Bar Council should adopt the disciplinary rules the Supreme Court has directed it to frame, making independent verification of every AI-sourced citation a precondition of filing, backed by investment in authenticated domestic legal databases so verification does not depend on proprietary systems beyond domestic reach.

kp.k: Shared infrastructure could counter unequal access to AI
kp.d: The author predicts that smaller firms and solo practitioners without enterprise-tool capital may fall further behind as litigants demand faster turnaround. As a policy response rather than an existing programme, she proposes government-backed shared AI infrastructure distributed through NALSA and state legal services authorities to legal aid providers and solo practitioners, aiming to prevent further widening of the access-to-justice gap.
qs: Smaller firms and solo practitioners, lacking the capital for enterprise AI tools, risk falling further behind even as litigants expect faster turnaround, widening the gap between large and small practices unless policy intervenes.

A government-backed shared AI infrastructure scheme, channelled through NALSA and state legal services authorities, would extend tools concentrated in large firms to legal aid providers and solo practitioners, keeping the access-to-justice gap from widening further.

kp.k: Cross-border AI processing raises unresolved confidentiality concerns
kp.d: The author argues that processing client material on infrastructure outside India raises attorney-client privilege questions unresolved by the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. She recommends incorporating the Supreme Court's disclosure duty into Bar Council professional standards and Ministry of Law and Justice review of the Advocates Act and data-protection legislation to address the claimed confidentiality gap.
qs: Confidentiality compounds the gap: AI systems often process client material on infrastructure outside India, raising questions the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 has not resolved for attorney-client privilege.

The Bar Council should mirror the Supreme Court's disclosure duty in its own Standards of Professional Conduct, while the Ministry of Law and Justice reviews the Advocates Act and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act to close the confidentiality gap around attorney-client privilege.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Zahoor argues that AI is changing the production of professional judgement, the economics and staffing of legal practice, and the responsibilities attached to legal work, rather than simply making lawyers redundant.
pts.d: Zahoor claims that automating repetitive research, drafting and document review removes work through which juniors traditionally acquired judgement. Client resistance to hourly charges for automatable work and growing fixed-fee arrangements weaken the revenue subsidy for apprenticeship. She predicts that large firms will hire fewer juniors for narrower purposes while expanding AI-supervision and legal-technology roles; specialist litigation, regulatory advice and courtroom advocacy will retain a premium. She argues that legal education must deliberately develop the reasoning and verification skills that routine work previously supplied. AI's benefits, she says, currently concentrate in large commercial firms, threatening to disadvantage smaller practices and widen unmet legal need. She also claims that fabricated authorities make independent human verification a discrete professional competency. Judicial deployment is expanding, but whether it reduces pendency rather than merely modernising administration remains unresolved. She identifies gaps in bar regulation of delegation, verification and confidentiality. Her proposals for shared infrastructure, district-court deployment, revised training and disciplinary safeguards are recommendations intended to shape these outcomes, not demonstrated effects of existing interventions.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Zahoor supports her argument with secondary survey findings, commercial adoption examples, reported hallucination incidents, institutional policies and deployment figures; the staffing and apprenticeship predictions are inferences rather than quantified employment findings.
pts.d: For pricing and staffing pressures, Zahoor cites the Thomson Reuters 2025 Future of Professionals report: 80 percent of respondents expect AI to change pricing, staffing and delivery, while roughly 90 percent of corporate outside-counsel spending remains hourly. These are reported expectations and a billing baseline, not measured AI-caused hiring reductions. She cites AZB & Partners' September 2025 firm-wide Harvey rollout for document review and translation, Shardul Amarchand Mangaldas' earlier partnership, Harvey's Bengaluru office, and a projection that India's legal services market will reach US$67.4 billion by 2030. She invokes the International Bar Association on junior-task exposure, Indian pedagogical commentary on lost cognitive effort, an OECD analysis on task reshaping rather than worker replacement, and Bar & Bench commentary on changing rewards for legal skills. For verification risks, she recounts the December 2024 Buckeye Trust order recall, a September 2025 Delhi High Court petition withdrawal, more than a hundred imaginary citations in an early-2026 commercial appeal, and a July 2026 Supreme Court decision involving six fabricated precedents. These are reported incidents and judicial responses, not measured model error rates. For deployment and governance, she cites more than 4,000 courts using Adalat AI, 53.57 crore rupees earmarked under eCourts Phase III, government descriptions of controlled pilots, Kerala's July 2025 policy, and the Supreme Court's June 2026 draft regulations. More than five crore pending cases, with over 85 percent in district and subordinate courts, establish the scale of the problem rather than an observed AI effect. The article supplies no quantified Indian hiring trend, training-outcome study or measured AI-driven pendency reduction.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Zahoor presents disruption as already underway in 2024–2026 and projects further change over the next decade, conditional on human supervision, institutional support and the distribution of access.
pts.d: The article treats firm adoption, fabricated-citation incidents and judicial rulemaking as current developments, drawing on examples from December 2024 through July 2026. Its staffing and specialisation forecasts concern the next decade without specifying annual rates or a precise endpoint. The 2030 market-size projection is a separate cited commercial forecast, not a forecast of AI-generated revenue. AI's contribution to judgement is explicitly conditional on lawyers critically checking outputs rather than accepting them wholesale. The forecast of widening differences between large and small practices is qualified by the possibility of policy intervention. The Supreme Court regulations discussed were draft rules, with a public-comment deadline extended from 20 June to 15 July 2026; their requirements should not be treated as already-final national rules. LegRAA and Digital Courts 2.1 are described as controlled pilots. Zahoor does not claim that scaling these systems will necessarily reduce case backlogs, and calls for pendency reduction to be the success measure. Her proposed shared infrastructure and training reforms are prospective responses to risks, with no quantified implementation schedule or demonstrated outcomes.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The predicted effects differ sharply between enterprise-equipped commercial firms, junior lawyers, smaller practices, legal aid providers and people dependent on overburdened lower courts.
pts.d: Zahoor frames the transition as affecting India's more than one million enrolled advocates, most outside the AI-equipped commercial tier. Junior associates face fewer routine drafting opportunities and earlier responsibility for supervising AI, while students risk missing the reasoning practice needed to exercise that supervision. Large firms gain access to enterprise tools and change their staffing and delivery models; specialist litigators, regulatory advisers and courtroom advocates are expected to retain market value. Smaller firms and solo practitioners face capital constraints and client expectations of faster turnaround. NALSA and other legal aid providers are described as excluded from the AI ecosystem, with consequences for people unable to obtain legal assistance, not merely for enterprise legal spending. Corporate clients influence pricing by resisting hourly charges for automatable work. Lawyers remain responsible for checking authorities, and client confidentiality is implicated when tools process privileged material outside India. Judges, court staff and litigants encounter transcription, research and case-management tools, but district and subordinate courts bear most of the backlog and may not share in higher-court efficiency gains. The Bar Council, universities, legal services authorities and government departments are assigned responsibility for education, access, discipline and safeguards.
